speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Ministers and other political appointment holders are notified of this Code at the start of each term of office and when a new political officeholder is appointed.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Code sets out guidelines on what constitutes private interests, requires Ministers to disclose these private interests and states that they should not influence or support issues in which they have a private interest.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Ministers are expected to be scrupulously above board and ensure no real or perceived conflict of interest between their official duties and private interests.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: As Prime Minister Lee had said in his Ministerial Statement earlier, the Prime Minister sends the Rules of Prudence after every election to all MPs of the PAP.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: These Rules set out clearly the conduct expected of the MPs, including the need to be proper and above board in their dealings with Government departments and public officers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: These Rules are also released to the media.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Public Service is also guided by a Code of Conduct that lays down the principles and rules that public officers must abide by.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This is periodically refreshed, and the Code of Conduct is available to all public officers in hard copies and on the Intranet.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Public officers must not undertake any activity that can give rise to any perception that official resources are being used for party political purposes.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Public officers are also expected to uphold the integrity and the reputation of the Public Service and public confidence in it.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Any request for information from the public is not granted automatically but would be carefully assessed on its merits.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: And this applies to members of the public who happen to be family members of political appointees as well.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: To ensure that public officers understand and uphold these values, the Code of Conduct is discussed in induction programmes for new public officers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Permanent Secretaries and Statutory Board Chief Executive Officers (CEOs) also lead town halls to explain the Code of Conduct to their officers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: These town halls include discussions to help officers understand how to interpret and live the code.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: As I had informed the House on several occasions, there are avenues for public officers to report suspected misconduct directly to their agency heads or Permanent Secretaries.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: They may also report to the Head of Civil Service, the Public Service Commission or to enforcement agencies, such as the Police or the Corrupt Practices Investigation Bureau.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Singapore and Singaporeans can justifiably be proud of the hard-earned reputation and long track record of integrity of our Public Service.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We are recognised for our record of integrity by Transparency International, by the World Economic Forum and the International Institute for Management Development (IMD) in their rankings on Global Competitiveness for the transparency and efficiency of our public institutions.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This is a key pillar of Government that Mr Lee Kuan Yew and our Pioneer leaders have built.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Public Service staunchly believes in and commits itself to living up to the high standards set by Mr Lee and his founding team.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Second, what is the work of the Committee?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: First, why did we set up this Committee?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: There is a significant public interest element involved when considering options for founding Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew's house at 38 Oxley Road.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: At the same time, the Government has also said that it will pay attention to respecting the wishes of Mr Lee for his house.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: These considerations are in addition to the due processes that take place for all buildings and structures with heritage and historical value.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: There is a misconception that the Government is seeking to make a decision now.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: It is merely preparing drawer plans of various options and their implications so that a future government can refer to them and make a considered and informed decision when the time comes to decide on the matter.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: And there is no decision required so long as Dr Lee continues staying in the house.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This is what Mr Lee wanted and expressed in his will.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: It might be 20 to 30 years later before a decision needs to be made.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: However, if Dr Lee chooses to leave earlier, say, within a few months, then the Cabinet and the Government will have to decide, and it would be useful to have studied the different options.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Some of us in Cabinet, including me, also felt that it would be a useful element for a future government deciding on the house if it had a set of options that came from Ministers who had personally discussed this matter with Mr Lee.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: As the Prime Minister had recused himself, I chair the Cabinet should any deliberations take place on this property.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Cabinet had recorded this at its meeting on 15 April 2015.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Prior to this, work on this issue had been carried out at staff level with interagency consultations as needed, with matters being surfaced by relevant Ministers to me or the Cabinet, without the Prime Minister, when necessary.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I had supported the Minister for National Development's proposal, as setting up such a Ministerial Committee would improve coordination and oversight on this matter.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I chair this Committee on the property at 38 Oxley Road, and included the relevant Cabinet Members, that is, the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth Grace Fu for heritage, the Minister for Law K Shanmugam for land issues, and the Minister for National Development Lawrence Wong for urban planning.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This Committee is like numerous other committees that the Cabinet may set up from time to time to study specific issues, for instance, on Smart Nation and Digital Government, Population, National Research and on Climate Change which I chair.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Tharman has provided examples of other committees that he chairs, such as for the Changi East Developments.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We even have a task force now looking at infant formula.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: They are all part of the normal working process of the Cabinet, or, indeed, the board of any large organisation.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We would rarely need to announce the formation of such committees, as they often relate to internal working processes and coordination within the Government.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This is similar in approach to Cabinet committees set up by many other governments.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: These committees ultimately report to the Cabinet, which operates under the principle of collective Cabinet responsibility.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This is an important consideration because members of Cabinet may have differing perspectives, but once the Cabinet decides, members take collective responsibility for the decision.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I will now elaborate on these three aspects of the Terms of Reference.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: With regard to the first aspect of the Terms of Reference for the Committee − why does the Government need to get involved in this matter at all?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Government has the responsibility to consider the public interest aspects of any property with historical and heritage significance and has a range of powers to gazette or acquire such property.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I should emphasise that the Government not only has the legal powers to act but, indeed, the responsibility to decide on what to do.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Ultimately, the government of the day has to decide and carry the decision.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Government has to carefully consider the merits for each property to be preserved or conserved.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Many of these predate our Independence and hark back to our early immigrant and colonial era, such as Admiralty House, the House of Tan Yeok Nee and the Sun Yat Sen Nanyang Memorial Hall.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We have precious few from our Independence era, and there have been calls to conserve these, such as several blocks of SIT flats in Tiong Bahru.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: For those who are not familiar with what "SIT" stands for, it is the Singapore Improvement Trust, the precursor of the Housing and Development Board.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: In the 1960s through to the 1980s, we cleared whole precincts and demolished many buildings for urban development, to make way for the new, in land-scarce Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: There was an urgent need for decent housing and industrial and commercial land for jobs − all for our people.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: When we look back, we were perhaps in some cases overzealous in doing so.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Indeed, as fewer such precincts or buildings remained, the value of each of them as a link to the past became more salient − old shophouses and warehouses, Peranakan houses, "black and whites", and Bukit Brown.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: With the passing years and fading memories, more Singaporeans, too, began to yearn to keep these gradually dwindling remaining physical links to our past, either for their architectural typology or the history they embody.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: In some cases, the property owners or members of the public argued to retain the buildings, for example, the old National Library building not so long ago, but they had to make way for development needs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: In other cases, owners applied for redevelopment but were directed to conserve the buildings for their historic or heritage value, often forgoing considerable financial gains they might have reaped from redevelopment.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: There is a due process for considering such matters and the decision is never taken lightly.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The ultimate decision is made by the Government.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: It was home to our founding Prime Minister.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: It was in its basement dining room that many important discussions and critical decisions on the future of Singapore were made by Mr Lee and our Pioneer leaders.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: As Mr Lee and our Pioneer generation of leaders − in fact, our Pioneer generation − pass on, the historical significance of markers of this period has grown. 38 Oxley Road is a key marker of this turning point in our history.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: A key consideration for 38 Oxley Road is Mr Lee's thinking on the property, which brings me to the second aspect of the Terms of Reference.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Committee has been paying particular attention to respecting Mr Lee Kuan Yew's wishes as we look at the range of possible options.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This is the reason why we had sought views from Mr Lee's children.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: It was a considered discussion where he presented his views and he listened to the views expressed by the Cabinet members.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: While Mr Lee expressed his personal wishes, he was also very proper.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: He was aware of the Government's responsibilities and how the law on this matter operates.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Earlier today, the Prime Minister read out to Members of this House the letter that Mr Lee had written to the Cabinet.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This was Mr Lee's last formal communication with the Cabinet on this matter.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Subsequently, as we have learnt from the beneficiaries of his estate, he had also expressed his wishes on the property in paragraph 7 of his last will.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This paragraph had two main limbs, with a third limb saying that this paragraph could be made public so that his wishes are known.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Indeed, it is only natural that the Committee should ask the siblings for their views.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The siblings wrote to us, providing differing views, including on the drafting of the last will.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We then provided each party two opportunities to comment on the views of the other party.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Indeed, the fact that the Committee received differing views showed how essential it was that we had sought the views of the siblings on Mr Lee's wishes and thinking.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: He has repeated the same allegations today, ignoring the replies that have been provided to him in writing, in fact, since the very beginning when he was first informed of the setting up of the Committee.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: If I may draw Members' attention to the response from my Press Secretary yesterday, and I seek Mdm Speaker's permission to circulate this response to Members.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Exchanges have happened quite rapidly, so, Mdm Speaker, I will read this out.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Committee sought Mr Lee Hsien Yang and Dr Lee Wei Ling's views on the late Mr Lee's wishes and thinking in July 2016.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In its initial letters, the Committee had made clear to Mr Lee Hsien Yang and Dr Lee Wei Ling the purpose and scope of the Committee's work.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This includes (a) why the Committee was formed, (b) who it reports to, namely, the Cabinet, (c) what it would look into, and (d) why Mr Lee Hsien Yang, Dr Lee Wei Ling and, of course, Mr Lee Hsien Loong's inputs would be useful.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Committee told him clearly that it was listing the various options for the house to present to Cabinet.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Committee was not going to make any recommendations.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I have enclosed letters dated 27 July 2016, shortly after the Committee was formed, and 24 August 2016 to Mr Lee Hsien Yang and Dr Lee Wei Ling, which made these points very clear.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, this was made very clear to Dr Lee and Mr Lee Hsien Yang on 25 April 2017.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I have not included that letter because I do not want to swamp Members with voluminous exchanges and letters.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Committee also made clear to Mr Lee Hsien Yang from the outset that his provision of any reply was purely voluntary.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: On this basis, Mr Lee Hsien Yang proceeded to make various submissions to the Committee, both last year and into this year.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The circumstances of the last will became relevant for a good reason, and this is because Mr Lee Hsien Yang's representations to the Committee placed reliance on one part of the last will as the primary evidence of Mr Lee's intent.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: He wanted the Committee to focus on one part of the clause relating to Mr Lee's wishes on the house and not the other parts.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: When the circumstances related to the drafting of the last will were brought to the Committee's attention, Mr Lee Hsien Yang's views on this were sought, and in the same vein − I might add − the Committee had also posed questions to Mr Lee Hsien Loong, some of them uncomfortable ones based on representations made by Mr Lee Hsien Yang and Dr Lee Wei Ling.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: First of all, Dr Lee Wei Ling and Mr Lee Hsien Yang knew about the Committee.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We informed them shortly after the Committee was formed on 27 July 2016.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We also informed them what the Committee was setting out to do − this was on 27 July 2016 and, in response to his questions, we expanded on that, gave him some reassurances.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And Members can see that from the letter on 24 August 2016.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: They were also invited to make representations to the Committee.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Committee was not looking at things in isolation.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Now, how can they be making representations to the Committee if this was a secret Committee and they did not know it existed?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: They gave their views and they offered them freely and voluntarily.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: They were also told clearly on 25 April 2017 that the Committee is not looking into the validity of the will, and its only interest is in understanding Mr Lee's wishes better.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, Mdm Speaker, going through the facts and the chronology, Dr Lee Wei Ling and Mr Lee Hsien Yang, we must then ask, are they being truthful and honest when they allege that this is some "secret" Committee which they did not know about, and which was only acknowledged after Dr Lee Wei Ling and Mr Lee Hsien Yang somehow exposed its existence?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: They were responding to it and sent several representations.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: They knew what the Committee was doing and, so, there is nothing mysterious about it, or there should not be.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: It was giving an opportunity for parties to express their views.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Consider if the Committee had not asked the siblings for their views, it would have been a significant omission and then, in such a situation, the siblings might be justifiably upset that the Committee had not given them an opportunity to make their views known, or to make clarifications which another party may have put in which differed from theirs.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But all the siblings were provided a full opportunity to do so.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The siblings should, therefore, really have no reason to be unhappy with being asked, being given the opportunity to make voluntary representations to offer their views and to make clarifications.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Our interest is confined to obtaining as full a picture as possible of Mr Lee's thinking on the house.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Now we have to decide: if we want to take Mr Lee's views into consideration, then we must understand what they were; if we decide that we are not going to take Mr Lee's views into consideration at all, then we do not need to ask.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But if we want to know and get as full a picture as possible as to what Mr Lee's were, then it is incumbent for the Committee to try to determine these as best as we can.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I should emphasise again that it is not for the Committee to decide whose claims are valid, in particular, over the validity of the will.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We had explained this, as I have said, on 25 April 2017 in writing to Mr Lee Hsien Yang and Dr Lee Wei Ling.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: What we do try is to understand, as best we can, Mr Lee's wishes and thinking.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We had also explained that all the representations and views offered were voluntary.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But we did tell all of them that any views provided would be useful and the Committee will consider all the views offered.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Indeed, soon after Mr Lee's passing, the allegations of "dynastic ambitions" and "abuse of power" were already being made, to many people, in smaller circles.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I know because several people spoke to me about having been approached and offered these allegations and views, and they expressed their concerns.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This was shortly after Mr Lee's passing, well before the formation of any committee.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In April 2016, before the Committee was formed, Dr Lee Wei Ling had made a public posting making such allegations.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I do not recall that Mr Lee Hsien Yang dissociated himself from these postings either.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Saying that the Committee has somehow now "pushed" Mr Lee Hsien Yang to take these allegations public, therefore, does not conform to the facts and chronology.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Both parties were offered opportunities to respond if they wished to.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This is being open and transparent with all the parties.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Being given the opportunity to voluntarily clarify issues even though they may be uncomfortable can hardly be considered an abuse of power.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Committee is not the reason for these differences.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Committee is merely trying to get the best understanding of Mr Lee's thinking on the property.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: As there are differences of views, it may be useful to have a contemporaneous record of what these are, so that they can be referred to, if needed, when a decision is needed to be taken eventually.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I should also point out that the Committee carried out its work through direct correspondence in writing with the siblings, and out of the public eye.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Committee did not think that it was useful for these differences to be aired in public.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But the siblings' views had relevance to the Committee's work because it helps the Committee take Mr Lee's wishes into account, along with the public interest aspects, when drawing up a range of options for the property.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We hope that the differences of views on private matters can be resolved within the family.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But, ultimately, the government of the day and its Ministers cannot avoid taking responsibility for making the required decisions on matters involving the public interest.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And this is why Singapore has laws that give the Government powers, specifically the Preservation of Monuments Act and the Planning Act in this case.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: As Members have asked, this does not preclude consultations or the involvement of some memorial committee at an appropriate time.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In fact, I think this will be useful.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Members of the public have already written in, offering suggestions.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: At the appropriate time, I will see how best to seek wider public views on this.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But I suppose I also have to weigh this against those who might jump to the conclusion that doing so means that the Government is imminently going to decide or to do something with the property when there is no need to decide now.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: If Prime Minister Lee had not recused himself and had simply, as the Prime Minister, ordered the Government agencies to demolish the house without due process, that would have been an abuse of authority and power.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: It would have bypassed the objective due process that Mr Lee himself would have stood for.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: It is ironic that following the proper process is now being labelled, by some, as an abuse of power.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Perhaps it is because they feel that their demand for a particular outcome should simply be carried out.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But simply doing this would be an abuse of power.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Going through due process is the proper way of doing things.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Anyone who has run a major listed company would or should know how companies deal with conflicts of interest, even where it involves the Chairman or CEO.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Take, for example, a property company that is going to bid for an en bloc redevelopment.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: If the Chairman or CEO happens to own apartment units in this development, they would have to recuse themselves.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Others in the company would then have to be empowered to decide on the bid.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We now come to the third aspect of the Terms of Reference of the Committee − the due process to develop possible plans and options for the property.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: No decision is required now on what to do with the property.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: As I said earlier, this was made clear to the siblings in writing that neither the Committee nor the Cabinet will make any decision on the House, and that the Committee is only listing and studying the various options, as drawer plans.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This will take some time and the Government has to study the options in advance of any eventualities.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: For instance, if Dr Lee chooses to move out of the house in the near future, the decision on what to do about the house might have to be taken at that point.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: On the options for the house, the Committee does not take a binary, "either or" approach.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Committee has no preconceived notion that the house must be kept as it is, or that it must be totally demolished.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I met Mr Lee Hsien Yang earlier five times in 2015, between 14 April and July 2015, and once more, the sixth time, in April 2016, on a range of issues.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The meetings were before the Ministerial Committee was formed.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: At one end, preserving the house as it is for visitors to enter and see the private spaces, would be totally against the wishes of Mr and Mrs Lee Kuan Yew.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And at the other end, demolishing the house and putting the property on the market to develop new private residences, such as luxury apartments.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The latter, redevelopment into private apartments, would not only result in the loss of a historically significant property, but also allow this very history to be exploited for private profit, for example, by marketing the residences as "living at the former house of Mr Lee Kuan Yew".

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I am certain many Singaporeans will have not approved of this.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Indeed, Mr Lee Hsien Yang has also acknowledged this, and on 1 July 2017, has said that he has no "inclination" to do so.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The dining room was where many important historical meetings were held to discuss how a self-governing Singapore would take shape.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I personally think there are merits in these intermediate options which could provide a good solution.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Mr Lee Hsien Yang has in his public statements also indicated that he is open to some of these options.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Mr Lee Hsien Yang also acknowledges that no decision is needed now as Dr Lee Wei Ling continues to live in the property.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This is also the position of the Government.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In his statement on 1 July, he also said that he recognises that "no man stands above the law".

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: As I have explained, the Government has a duty to go through due process for when a decision needs to be taken, at some future time.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, there should really be no reason to disagree with what the Committee is doing.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We are studying the possible options for the time when a decision has to be made.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Mr Lee Hsien Yang now owns the property.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: As provided for in Mr Lee Kuan Yew's will, Dr Lee Wei Ling can stay in it for as long as she wishes.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And we have said we will not do anything to affect Dr Lee's right to continue living there.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: There is no decision required of this Government so long as Dr Lee stays there and the house is properly maintained, as provided for under the Building Control Act and the Planning Act.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Even if the Government were to take a position today, it would not bind a future government at the time when that future government has to make a decision and implement it.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We cannot take a prospective decision and say, "30 years from now, the future government will do this." Because the future government has the powers under the law to decide for itself.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: While there is no urgency to complete these studies within a specified timeframe − these are drawer plans which would be reviewed periodically − I will consult my colleagues to see if it is useful to put out a range of possibilities, to let the public ponder on the matter without having to arrive at any decision.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Emotions on this issue are still very strong, not just within the family, but also among some Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Emotions have sadly been heightened again by this public disagreement.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: A period of calm would be useful for reflection.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: With the passage of time, I hope that we will be able to arrive at a wise decision on this matter in an informed and considered way that takes into account the significant public interest to preserve the heritage of our young nation, while respecting Mr Lee's personal wishes for the house.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I explained that the Ministerial Committee was formed to examine (a) the historical and heritage significance of the property, (b) the wishes of Mr Lee Kuan Yew in relation to the property, and (c) the possible plans for the property and the neighbourhood, and the options to move forward.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: These are all matters which the Government has to take responsibility for and has to plan for.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This is just the normal process of the Government doing its work in a calm, objective and proper way.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In the coming days, we will fully debate the specific allegations that have been made against the Government and examine whether there is any substance behind them.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We do not bend to the private demands of individuals, no matter who they are, or what family connections they can claim.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This is the foundation upon which Mr Lee Kuan Yew and his team built our Singapore for all of us.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Mr Lee would have expected no less from us.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This is the Singapore that we want to continue living in.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And this is the Singapore that Prime Minister Lee, our Cabinet colleagues and I, and all our public officers in our agencies will fight to uphold and take forward.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We have many real challenges, and much to do.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Let us all focus together on these and work together to continue to serve Singaporeans and bring Singapore forward.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: That is what Mr Lee would have wanted us to do, more than anything else.
